method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia' (published 28 June 2024), 20 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11274906). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x) 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia' (published March 2022), 13 claims; LICENCE: © Springer Nature Limited 2021 (free to read at nature.com; no open licence) (read at the copyright line in the article PDF downloaded from nature.com (Unpaywall: free to read, no licence)). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the 2022 International Consensus Statement (modified Delphi, 160 statements; led from Melbourne), for general lifelong care, which S1 does not cover. S2 is © Springer Nature and free to read, so it is paraphrased and hash-anchored; text is from pdftotext of the published PDF, whose citation superscripts run into the words. The meeting was sponsored by BioMarin (maker of vosoritide), which the authors say had no input into content. The S1 claims are unchanged.

claims.claim: **Vosoritide is a C-type natriuretic peptide analogue, given by daily subcutaneous injection,** that counters FGFR3 signalling and increases endochondral bone growth.
claims.source_text: Vosoritide, an engineered C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) analogue, activates B-type natriuretic peptide receptor signalling with the inhibition of FGFR3 downstream signalling, leading to the promotion of chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation, and subsequent increased endochondral bone formation [,]. It has a longer half-life than endogenous CNP, allowing for daily subcutaneous administration.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Phase 3 trials showed a gain of 1.57 cm/year in annualised growth velocity** in children aged 5 and over, sustained over 3 years.
claims.source_text: Phase 3 clinical trials of vosoritide demonstrated an increase in annualised growth velocity of 1.57 cm/year in children with achondroplasia aged 5 years and older, which were sustained over 3 years
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Starting in infancy may reduce the risk of foramen magnum stenosis;** its effect on the foramen magnum under age 2 is still being studied.
claims.source_text: Thus, vosoritide may reduce the risk of foramen magnum stenosis if treatment is begun in infancy. The effects of vosoritide on the foramen magnum in infants aged <2 years are currently under investigation
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Confirm the diagnosis genetically:** testing must show the FGFR3 Gly380Arg mutation. If genetic testing is negative, do not start vosoritide; refer for further diagnostic work-up. (E)
claims.source_text: Genetic testing must confirm the Gly380Arg mutation in the FGFR3 gene. … If genetic testing is negative, vosoritide should not be started and the patient should be appropriately referred for further diagnostic work-up.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Growth plates must be open,** shown by knee X-rays or by growth velocity above 1.5 cm/year over at least 6 months; the X-ray route is more practical in infants under 6 months.
claims.source_text: Additionally, patients must not have evidence of growth plate closure as demonstrated by at least one of the following: … An annual growth velocity of greater than 1.5 cm/year as assessed over a period of at least 6 months. … the X-ray criteria are more practical in infants under 6 months.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat severe complications first:** craniocervical junction or spinal cord stenosis or compression, spinal deformity and sleep-disordered breathing should be managed before starting. **Infants need a sleep study and a craniocervical junction MRI beforehand.** (R)
claims.source_text: If the patient has severe complications of achondroplasia (craniocervical junction/spinal cord stenosis or compression, spinal deformities, sleep disordered breathing), appropriate medical or surgical management should be undertaken before initiating vosoritide. … Infants should undergo a sleep study and an MRI of the craniocervical junction prior to starting vosoritide treatment.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Optimise other conditions that affect growth (e.g. hypothyroidism).** Cardiac disease, conditions predisposing to hypotension and blood-pressure-lowering medicines raise the risk of symptomatic hypotension and may need closer monitoring at first doses.
claims.source_text: Patients should be assessed for any medical condition that could affect growth (e.g., hypothyroidism), and treatment should be optimised before initiating vosoritide. Patients who have cardiac conditions, other conditions predisposing to hypotension or who are taking medications associated with low blood pressure may be at an increased risk of symptomatic hypotension from vosoritide and may require closer monitoring on initial drug delivery.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Educate and train the family** on benefits, side effects, daily injection, refrigerated storage, reconstitution and site rotation. Safety is established only when at least 90% of prescribed doses are given. Obtain informed consent before prescribing. (E)
claims.source_text: Recommendation 3: Patients and families should be educated on the potential benefits and side effects of vosoritide, expected outcomes based on age, the need for daily drug administration, adequate storage and refrigeration of vosoritide, regular assessments, follow-up visits, attendance at the training session and the need for long-term monitoring (E). … the safety profile of the drug has only been established in cases where ≥90% of the prescribed doses are given, and the effects of irregular dosing patterns are unknown. … Recommendation 5: Informed consent from the parent/caregiver and child (if capable of understanding the education) to start therapy with vosoritide should be obtained prior to prescription (E).
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Dose by weight,** using the dosing calculator and the weight–dose band tables in the Product Information.
claims.source_text: The initial dose of vosoritide should be calculated based on patient weight, with reference to the dosing calculator [], and weight-dose band tables
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Give the first dose under supervision and observe for at least 2 hours** (1 hour can be considered from age 6 if stable). Check pulse and blood pressure before the dose, at 15 and 30 minutes, then every 30 minutes; symptomatic hypotension needs medical review. (E)
claims.source_text: The patients should be observed for a minimum of 2 h as the half-life of the drug is 28 min. Observation of 1 h for older children (aged 6 years and older) can be considered if there are no complications and the patients are medically stable. Pulse and blood pressure should be checked pre-dose, at 15 and 30 min post-injection, and then every 30 min until the observation period ends. … If the child has symptomatic hypotension, a medical review is required.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hypotension is very common but usually asymptomatic and self-limiting.**
claims.source_text: Hypotension is a very common adverse event; however, it is usually asymptomatic and self-resolves
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **First follow-up at 2–4 weeks** to check adverse events, injection technique, tolerance and adherence; it can be by phone or video if safe. (R)
claims.source_text: Recommendation 7: The first follow-up consultation is recommended at 2-4 weeks after the first dose of vosoritide to check for adverse events, injection technique, tolerance, patient compliance, challenges with drug administration and to answer any further questions (R). … The first follow-up consultation could be offered by telephone or video call if this is deemed safe by the treating medical specialist.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Review growth, achondroplasia complications, efficacy and safety from 6 months, then at 6-monthly and annual visits,** measuring height with a calibrated stadiometer every time. (E)
claims.source_text: The ongoing monitoring visits should commence 6 months after the first dose of vosoritide and then should include 6-monthly and annual visits (E). … Anthropometric measurements (Supplementary Material S4) to measure height should be conducted at every visit by using calibrated stadiometers
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Shared care with a local paediatrician or paediatric endocrinologist is reasonable for interim visits** once a child aged 2 or over is established, but annual visits stay in the specialist achondroplasia clinic. (R)
claims.source_text: When children aged 2 years and older have been established on vosoritide treatment, if the treating achondroplasia specialist considers it safe, they could be co-managed by a general paediatrician for their interim visits. … However, annual visits should be completed in the specialist achondroplasia clinic, which includes specialist nursing and allied health input.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Watch for worsening spinal deformity and slipped upper femoral epiphysis,** which can come with accelerated growth. Report suspected serious adverse events to the TGA (Black Triangle Scheme).
claims.source_text: a report submitted to the TGA under the Black Triangle Scheme. … Identifying worsening spinal deformity and slipped upper capital femoral epiphyses is important as these can be associated with accelerated growth.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Growth below 1.5 cm/year before late puberty needs urgent investigation.** Typical growth in achondroplasia is about 4 cm/year; poor response despite open growth plates may reflect scoliosis, knee varus or rarely growth hormone deficiency.
claims.source_text: If a child's growth slows to less than 1.5 cm/year before late puberty, urgent investigations into the causes of growth failure are required. … The typical growth velocity in children with achondroplasia is around 4 cm/year … Patients who are not responding to vosoritide despite open growth plates should be assessed for conditions like significant scoliosis and knee varus deformities that can result in reduced standing height. Rare unrelated conditions such as growth hormone deficiency may need to be excluded.
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspend vosoritide when low blood pressure is a risk,** such as reduced fluid intake in severe intercurrent illness and around surgery (until out of recovery). (R)
claims.source_text: Recommendation 11: Treatment should be suspended if the patient has, or is at risk of, low blood pressure; for example, when fluid intake is reduced during severe intercurrent illness and during the perioperative period (suspend until out of recovery) (R).
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stop when X-ray shows growth plate closure, or when growth is below 1.5 cm/year in late puberty on two consecutive measures over at least 6 months.**
claims.source_text: Vosoritide should be stopped if patients show evidence of growth plate closure on an X-ray or have an annual growth velocity of less than 1.5 cm/year in late puberty on two consecutive measures over at least 6 months
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Under 28 days old, the second dose is also supervised in a specialist clinic, with 4 hours' observation after each of the first two doses.** (E)
claims.source_text: Recommendation 12: In babies aged <28 days, in addition to the first dose, the second dose of vosoritide should also be administered under medical supervision in a specialist clinic and the observation period post-dose should be 4 h for both the first and the second doses (E).
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Under 24 months, all monitoring visits happen in a specialist clinic, with a formal review 3 months after starting;** measure supine length in children who cannot stand. (R)
claims.source_text: Recommendation 13: In babies and infants < 24 months of age, all monitoring visits (6-monthly and annual) should take place in a specialist clinic (R). … a formal review in the specialised clinic should occur 3 months after starting vosoritide. … For young children who are unable to stand independently, supine length measurements are needed
claims.locator: Australian Vosoritide Working Group, Children (MDPI) 2024;11(7):789, 'Consensus Guidelines for the Use of Vosoritide in Children with Achondroplasia in Australia', published 28 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11274906/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer every infant to a skeletal dysplasia centre or achondroplasia expert at diagnosis,** with ongoing multidisciplinary follow-up. In the first year, review every 2–4 months at first and then every 3–6 months.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Check for cervicomedullary compression at every visit in infants and young children:** motor regression or delayed milestones, apnoea, swallowing difficulty, poor weight gain, clonus, abnormal reflexes, weakness. Concerning findings need urgent paediatric neurosurgical review.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Consider an MRI of the cervicomedullary junction and foramen magnum in the first months of life, even without symptoms.** Symptomatic compression is an indication for foramen magnum decompression; MRI-proven compression without symptoms still needs a neurosurgical opinion.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Do a sleep study (polysomnography) in the first year or at the first sign of sleep-disordered breathing, and by 2 years at the latest.** Adenotonsillectomy is first-line for obstructive sleep apnoea, with a repeat study 2–4 months afterwards.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Teach positioning and handling:** avoid early unsupported sitting (fixed thoracolumbar kyphosis) and prolonged car-seat positioning (positional death). Refer to a paediatric spine surgeon if a kyphosis persists beyond a year or progresses once walking.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Use achondroplasia-specific growth charts,** and plot head circumference monthly through the first year.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Middle-ear effusions are common:** screen hearing at least yearly in early childhood and refer to ENT when concerned. Grommets can be recommended for effusions lasting 3 months or more with documented hearing loss.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Bracing does not treat genu varum.** Limb lengthening needs multidisciplinary assessment before and after, with psychological input.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Adults: back pain with neurological features** (claudication, spasticity, shorter walking distance, bladder or bowel change) suggests spinal stenosis: consider whole-spine MRI, and refer promptly to an experienced spine centre if the cord is compressed.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Measure adult blood pressure regularly with a correctly sized cuff,** or on the forearm if elbow contractures or short upper arms prevent it.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Pregnancy:** obstetrician-led care (not midwife-only) and an antenatal anaesthetic assessment; birth after 32 weeks should be by caesarean section because of pelvic shape and size.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Anaesthesia:** minimise head and neck movement during bag-mask ventilation and intubation because of foramen magnum stenosis, and have difficult-airway equipment ready.
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Inheritance for counselling:** about 80% of cases are new (de novo) variants in unaffected parents; 20% are inherited. One affected parent gives a 50% chance per child; with two affected parents it is 25% average stature, 50% achondroplasia and 25% homozygous (usually lethal).
claims.locator: Savarirayan R, Ireland P, Irving M et al. (International Achondroplasia Consensus Statement Group, 55 experts from 16 countries), Nature Reviews Endocrinology 18:173-189 (doi 10.1038/s41574-021-00595-x), 'International Consensus Statement on the diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and lifelong care of individuals with achondroplasia', published March 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-021-00595-x, retrieved 2026-09-24
